title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 114 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 572–574 (Night 114, continuing directly from nights-113), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 114 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. On the appointed day he returns to the lane; the woman at the window shows him her open palm, a mirror and a red kerchief, and vanishes without a word. At home his cousin ʿAzīza, weeping over a poem of her own unrequited love, reads the signs for him: come back in five days, and wait at the dyer's shop for her messenger. He wastes away for the five days while ʿAzīza nurses him and tells him tales of lovers. But the day is a Saturday, the Jewish dyer's shop is shut, and no one comes. He returns home to find ʿAzīza reciting another lament; when she asks, smiling, why he did not spend the night with his beloved, he kicks her, and she falls against a peg that cuts open her brow. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourteenth after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fourteenth night,
sentences.n: al-rābiʿata ʿashara, “fourteenth”: the print again has the masculine عشر beside the feminine night, and it is vocalised as printed.

sentences.t: قَٰلَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الشَّابَّ قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَلَمَّا انْقَضَى الْيَوْمَانِ قَالَتْ لِي ابْنَةُ عَمِّي طِبْ نَفْسًا وَقَرَّ عَيْنًا وَقَوِّ عَزْمَكَ وَالْبَسْ ثِيَابَكَ وَتَوَجَّهْ إِلَيْهَا عَلَى الْمِيعَادِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba qāla li-tāji al-mulūki fa-lammā inqaḍā al-yawmāni qālat lī ibnatu ʿammī ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan wa-qawwi ʿazmaka wa-ilbas thiyābaka wa-tawajjah ilayhā ʿalā al-mīʿādi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the youth said to Tāj al-Mulūk: So when the two days were over, the daughter of my uncle said to me: Be good of soul and cool of eye, and strengthen your resolve, and put on your clothes and go to her at the appointment.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the young man said to Tāj al-Mulūk: When the two days were over, my cousin said to me, “Take heart and be glad, be firm of purpose; put on your clothes and go to her at the appointed time.”
sentences.n: The print writes qālat, “she said”, short, as قلت; the small upright alif restores the long vowel without changing the letters. ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan, “be good of soul and cool of eye”: two set phrases of comfort, each an imperative with an accusative of specification (nafsan, ʿaynan, “as to soul, as to eye”). A cool eye is a glad one, as a hot eye is a weeping one. li-tāji al-mulūki: li-, “to”, marking whom he speaks to.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا قَامَتْ وَغَيَّرَتْ أَثْوَابِي وَبَخَّرَتْنِي
sentences.tr: thumma innahā qāmat wa-ghayyarat athwābī wa-bakhkharatnī
sentences.l: Then she rose and changed my clothes and censed-me.
sentences.i: Then she got up, changed my clothes, and perfumed me with incense.
sentences.n: bakhkharatnī, “she censed me”: she held burning incense (bakhūr) about him so that the smoke scented his clothes.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَدَدْتُ حَيْلِي وَقَوَّيْتُ قَلْبِي وَخَرَجْتُ وَتَمَشَّيْتُ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلْتُ الزُّقَاقَ وَجَلَسْتُ عَلَى الْمِصْطَبَةِ سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: thumma shadadtu ḥaylī wa-qawwaytu qalbī wa-kharajtu wa-tamashshaytu ilā an dakhaltu al-zuqāqa wa-jalastu ʿalā al-miṣṭabati sāʿatan
sentences.l: Then I tightened my strength and strengthened my heart, and went-out and walked until I entered the lane, and sat on the bench an hour.
sentences.i: Then I gathered my strength and steadied my heart, and went out and walked until I came into the lane, and sat on the stone bench for a while.
sentences.n: ḥayl, “strength”, is the colloquial form of ḥawl, and shadda ḥaylahu, “he tightened his strength”, is a spoken idiom for bracing oneself. The miṣṭaba is the raised stone bench built against a house or shop front, where he sat two days before.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالطَّاقَةِ قَدِ انْفَتَحَتْ فَنَظَرْتُ بِعَيْنِي إِلَيْهَا فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهَا وَقَعْتُ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-ṭāqati qadi infataḥat fa-naẓartu bi-ʿaynī ilayhā fa-lammā raʾaytuhā waqaʿtu maghshiyyan ʿalayya
sentences.l: And behold, the window had opened; so I looked with my eye at her, and when I saw her I fell fainted-upon-me.
sentences.i: And suddenly the little window opened, and I looked up at her, and when I saw her I fell down in a faint.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-al-ṭāqati: idhā of surprise, “and behold”, with bi- marking what appears; it does not mean “with” here. bi-ʿaynī, “with my eye”: bi- of the instrument. maghshiyyan ʿalayya, literally “covered over upon me”, is the stock phrase for fainting; the print marks the shadda of ʿalayya.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَفَقْتُ فَشَدَدْتُ عَزْمِي وَقَوَّيْتُ قَلْبِي وَنَظَرْتُ إِلَيْهَا ثَانِيًا فَغِبْتُ عَنِ الْوُجُودِ ثُمَّ اسْتَفَقْتُ
sentences.tr: thumma afaqtu fa-shadadtu ʿazmī wa-qawwaytu qalbī wa-naẓartu ilayhā thāniyan fa-ghibtu ʿani al-wujūdi thumma istafaqtu
sentences.l: Then I came-to, and tightened my resolve and strengthened my heart, and looked at her a second time, and was absent from existence; then I came-round.
sentences.i: Then I came to, braced my resolve, steadied my heart, and looked at her a second time — and lost all sense of the world; then I came round again.
sentences.n: ghibtu ʿani al-wujūdi, “I was absent from existence”, is a phrase for losing consciousness, used too of mystical rapture. afaqtu and istafaqtu both mean “I recovered”: the second is the tenth form of the same root.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ مَعَهَا مِرْآةً وَمِنْدِيلًا أَحْمَرَ وَحِينَ رَأَتْنِي شَمَّرَتْ عَنْ سَاعِدَيْهَا وَفَتَحَتْ أَصَابِعَهَا الْخَمْسَ وَدَقَّتْ بِهَا عَلَى صَدْرِهَا بِالْكَفِّ وَالْخَمْسِ أَصَابِعَ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu maʿahā mirʾātan wa-mindīlan aḥmara wa-ḥīna raʾatnī shammarat ʿan sāʿidayhā wa-fataḥat aṣābiʿahā al-khamsa wa-daqqat bihā ʿalā ṣadrihā bi-al-kaffi wa-al-khamsi aṣābiʿa
sentences.l: And I saw with her a mirror and a red kerchief; and when she saw me she rolled-up (her sleeves) from her two forearms, and opened her fingers, the five, and struck with them on her breast, with the palm and the five fingers.
sentences.i: I saw that she had a mirror and a red kerchief with her. When she saw me, she bared her forearms, spread the five fingers of her hand, and struck her breast with them, palm and five fingers together.
sentences.n: shammarat ʿan sāʿidayhā, “she rolled up from her forearms”: the sleeves are understood. bihā, “with them”: bi- of the instrument. al-khamsi aṣābiʿa, “the five fingers”: the article goes on the numeral rather than on the counted noun, a usage of the spoken language that recurs in this tale.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَفَعَتْ يَدَيْهَا وَأَبْرَزَتِ الْمِرْآةَ مِنَ الطَّاقَةِ وَأَخَذَتِ الْمِنْدِيلَ الْأَحْمَرَ وَدَخَلَتْ بِهِ وَعَادَتْ وَاَدْلَتْهُ مِنَ الطَّاقَةِ إِلَى صَوْبِ الزُّقَاقِ ثَلٰثَ مَرَّاتٍ وَهِيَ تُدَلِّيهِ وَتَرْفَعُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma rafaʿat yadayhā wa-abrazati al-mirʾāta mina al-ṭāqati wa-akhadhati al-mindīla al-aḥmara wa-dakhalat bihi wa-ʿādat wa-adlathu mina al-ṭāqati ilā ṣawbi al-zuqāqi thalātha marrātin wa-hiya tudallīhi wa-tarfaʿuhu
sentences.l: Then she raised her two hands and put-forth the mirror from the window, and took the red kerchief and went-in with it, and came-back and let-it-down from the window toward the lane three times, she lowering it and raising it.
sentences.i: Then she raised both hands and held the mirror out of the window; then she took the red kerchief, went in with it, came back, and let it down from the window towards the lane three times, lowering it and drawing it up again.
sentences.n: dakhalat bihi, “she went in with it”: bi- here means “with, carrying”, the verb of motion plus bi- meaning to take something along. The print itself points the first two letters of wa-adlathu, “and she let it down” (وَاَ), with a plain fatḥa and no hamza; that is kept. thalātha, “three”, is spelled short as ثلث, as often in this edition.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ عَصَرَتْهُ وَلَفَّتْهُ بِيَدِهَا وَطَأْطَأَتْ رَأْسَهَا ثُمَّ جَذَبَتْهَا مِنَ الطَّاقَةِ وَأَغْلَقَتِ الطَّاقَةَ وَانْصَرَفَتْ وَلَمْ تُكَلِّمْنِي كَلِمَةً وَاحِدَةً بَلْ تَرَكَتْنِي حَيْرَانًا لَا أَعْلَمُ مَا أَشَارَتْ بِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma ʿaṣarathu wa-laffathu bi-yadihā wa-ṭaʾṭaʾat raʾsahā thumma jadhabathā mina al-ṭāqati wa-aghlaqati al-ṭāqata wa-inṣarafat wa-lam tukallimnī kalimatan wāḥidatan bal tarakatnī ḥayrānan lā aʿlamu mā ashārat bihi
sentences.l: Then she wrung it and wound it in her hand, and bowed her head; then she drew it (f.) from the window, and closed the window and went-away, and did not speak to me one word, but left me bewildered, not knowing what she signed with.
sentences.i: Then she wrung it, wound it round her hand, and bowed her head; then she drew back from the window, shut it and was gone, without saying a single word to me, and left me bewildered, not knowing what her signs meant.
sentences.n: jadhabathā, “she drew it back”: the pronoun is feminine, and nothing feminine is near but her hand or the window itself; most likely she drew her hand, or herself, back in. ḥayrānan, “bewildered”: the print spells it with a final alif, i.e. with the -an ending, where Classical usage would have ḥayrāna. mā ashārat bihi, “what she signed with”: ashāra bi-, “to make a sign of, indicate”; the verb takes bi-.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَمَرَّيْتُ جَالِسًا إِلَى وَقْتِ الْعِشَاءِ ثُمَّ جِئْتُ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ قُرْبَ نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ فَوَجَدْتُ ابْنَةَ عَمِّي وَاضِعَةً يَدَهَا عَلَى خَدِّهَا وَأَجْفَانُهَا تَسْكُبُ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَهِيَ تُنْشِدُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-istamarraytu jālisan ilā waqti al-ʿishāʾi thumma jiʾtu ilā al-bayti qurba niṣfi al-layli fa-wajadtu ibnata ʿammī wāḍiʿatan yadahā ʿalā khaddihā wa-ajfānuhā taskubu al-ʿabarāti wa-hiya tunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And I continued sitting till the time of the night-prayer; then I came to the house near the middle of the night, and found the daughter of my uncle placing her hand on her cheek, and her eyelids pouring tears, and she reciting these verses:
sentences.i: I stayed sitting there until the hour of the night prayer, and then came home towards midnight, and found my cousin with her cheek in her hand and her eyes streaming with tears, reciting these verses:
sentences.n: istamarraytu, “I continued”, is the spoken form of Classical istamrartu, as if the verb ended in a weak letter; the print marks its shadda. al-ʿishāʾ is the evening prayer, after nightfall.

sentences.t:
مَا لِيْ وَلِلَّاحِيْ عَلَيْكَ يُعَنِّفُ * كَيْفَ السُّلُوُّ وَانْتَ غُصْنٌ اَهْيَفُ
يَا طَلْعَةً سَلَبَتْ فُؤَادِيْ وَانْثَنَتْ * مَا لِلْهَوَى الْعُذْرِيِّ عَنْهَا مَصْرِفُ
تُرْكِيَّةُ الْاَلْحَاظِ تَفْعَلُ بِالْحَشَى * مَا لَيْسَ يَفْعَلُهُ الصَّقِيلُ الْمُرْهَفُ
حَمَّلْتِنِي ثِقْلَ الْغَرَامِ وَلَيْسَ لِي * جَلَدٌ عَلَى حَمْلِ الْقَمِيصِ وَاَضْعَفُ
وَلَقَدْ بَكَيْتُ دَمًا لِقَوْلِ عَوَاذِلِي * مِنْ جَفْنِ مَنْ تَهْوَى يَرُوعُكَ مُرْهَفُ
يَا لَيْتَ قَلْبِي مِثْلَ قَلْبِكَ اِنَّمَا * جِسْمِي كَخَصْرِكَ بِالنَّحَافَةِ مُتْلَفُ
لَكَ يَا اَمِيْرِىْ فِى الْمَلَاحَةِ نَاظِرٌ * صَعْبٌ عَلَيَّ وَحَاجِبٌ لَا يَنْصِفُ
كَذَبَ الَّذِي قَالَ الْمَلَاحَةُ كُلُّهَا * فِي يُوسُفٍ كَمْ فِي جَمَالِكَ يُوسُفُ
اَتَكَلَّفُ الْاِعْرَاضَ عَنْكَ مَخَافَةً * مِنْ اَعْيُنِ الرُّقَبَاءِ كَمْ اَتَكَلَّفُ
sentences.tr:
mā lī wa-li-al-lāḥī ʿalayka yuʿannifu * kayfa al-sulūwu wa-anta ghuṣnun ahyafu
yā ṭalʿatan salabat fuʾādī wa-inthanat * mā li-al-hawā al-ʿudhriyyi ʿanhā maṣrifu
turkiyyatu al-alḥāẓi tafʿalu bi-al-ḥashā * mā laysa yafʿaluhu al-ṣaqīlu al-murhafu
ḥammaltinī thiqla al-gharāmi wa-laysa lī * jaladun ʿalā ḥamli al-qamīṣi wa-aḍʿafu
wa-laqad bakaytu daman li-qawli ʿawādhilī * min jafni man tahwā yarūʿuka murhafu
yā layta qalbī mithla qalbika innamā * jismī ka-khaṣrika bi-al-naḥāfati mutlafu
laka yā amīrī fī al-malāḥati nāẓirun * ṣaʿbun ʿalayya wa-ḥājibun lā yanṣifu
kadhaba alladhī qāla al-malāḥatu kulluhā * fī yūsufin kam fī jamālika yūsufu
atakallafu al-iʿrāḍa ʿanka makhāfatan * min aʿyuni al-ruqabāʾi kam atakallafu
sentences.l:
What is it to me, and to the blamer who reproaches (me) over you? How (can there be) forgetting, when you are a slender bough?
O face that robbed my heart and swayed-away — the ʿUdhrī love has no turning-away from it.
Turkish of glances, it does to the entrails what the polished keen-edged (blade) does not do.
You have loaded me with the weight of passion, and I have no endurance for the bearing of the shirt, and I am weaker (still).
And I have wept blood at the saying of my blamers: From the eyelid of the one you love a keen-edged (blade) alarms you.
Would that my heart were like your heart! Only my body, like your waist, is wasted with thinness.
You have, O my prince, in beauty, an overseer hard upon me, and a chamberlain who does not deal justly.
He lied who said: Beauty, all of it, is in Joseph — how many a Joseph is in your beauty!
I force myself to the turning-away from you, for fear of the eyes of the watchers — how much I force myself!
sentences.i:
What have I to do with the critic who scolds me over you? How could I forget, when you are a slender, swaying bough?
O face that stole my heart and turned away — no chaste love can ever turn from it.
Those Turkish glances do to the heart what the keenest polished sword could never do.
You have laid the whole weight of passion on me, and I have no strength to bear even my shirt; I am weaker still.
I wept blood when my critics said, “The eyelids of the one you love hold a blade to frighten you.”
If only my heart were like yours! It is only my body that, like your waist, is worn away to nothing.
In beauty, my prince, you keep an eye that is harsh with me and a brow that gives no justice.
He lied who said that all beauty was in Joseph: how many Josephs there are in your beauty!
I make myself turn away from you for fear of the watchers' eyes — and how hard I make myself!
sentences.n: ʿUdhrī love is the chaste, hopeless love of the poets of the tribe of ʿUdhra, who were said to die of it. A “Turkish” glance is a narrow-eyed, killing one: the Turks were the archers and soldiers of the age, and their beauty a commonplace. In the seventh line nāẓir is both “eye” and “overseer”, and ḥājib both “eyebrow” and “chamberlain”, the officer who keeps petitioners from a ruler: the beloved's eye and brow are officials who will not let the lover in. The print points yanṣifu where Classical has yunṣifu, and gives yūsufin a full ending, which the metre requires. The poem speaks to a man (anta, jamālika), but the print points ḥammaltinī, “you have loaded me”, as addressed to a woman; that is kept. Joseph, the son of Jacob, whose beauty the Qurʾān tells of (Sura 12), is the type of male beauty. bi-al-ḥashā: bi-, “to”, after faʿala, “do (something) to”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ شِعْرَهَا زَادَ مَا بِي مِنَ الْهُمُومِ وَتَكَاثَرَتْ عَلَيَّ الْغُمُومُ وَوَقَعْتُ فِي زَوَايَا الْبَيْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu shiʿrahā zāda mā bī mina al-humūmi wa-takātharat ʿalayya al-ghumūmu wa-waqaʿtu fī zawāyā al-bayti
sentences.l: So when I heard her verse, what was in me of cares increased, and the griefs multiplied upon me, and I fell in the corners of the house.
sentences.i: When I heard her poem, the cares I carried grew greater and the griefs crowded in on me, and I fell down in a corner of the house.
sentences.n: al-humūm … al-ghumūm, “cares … griefs”: a rhyming pair, as the narrative often has. mā bī, “what was in me”: bi- here means “in”. The print marks the -tu of samiʿtu and the shadda of ʿalayya.

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَتْ إِلَيَّ وَحَمَلَتْنِي وَقَلَعَتْنِي أَثْوَابِي وَمَسَحَتْ وَجْهِي بِكُمِّهَا ثُمَّ سَأَلَتْنِي عَنْ مَاجَرَي لِي فَحَكَيْتُ لَهَا جَمِيعَ مَا حَصَلَ لِي مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍat ilayya wa-ḥamalatnī wa-qalaʿatnī athwābī wa-masaḥat wajhī bi-kummihā thumma saʾalatnī ʿan mā jarā lī fa-ḥakaytu lahā jamīʿa mā ḥaṣala lī minhā
sentences.l: And she rose to me and carried me and stripped-me my clothes, and wiped my face with her sleeve; then she asked me about what had happened to me, and I related to her all that had come to me from her (the lady).
sentences.i: She came to me, lifted me up, took off my clothes and wiped my face with her sleeve; then she asked me what had happened, and I told her everything the woman had done.
sentences.n: qalaʿatnī athwābī, “she stripped me my clothes”: the verb takes two objects, the person and the clothes, a spoken construction. bi-kummihā: bi-, “with”, of the instrument. mājarā, “what happened”, is printed as one word, with a dotted final yā. minhā, “from her”, means from the woman at the window.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يَابْنَ عَمِّي أَمَّا إِشَارَتُهَا بِالْكَفِّ وَالْخَمْسَةِ أَصَابِعَ فَإِنَّ تَفْسِيرَهُ تَعَالَ بَعْدَ خَمْسَةِ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat yā-bna ʿammī ammā ishāratuhā bi-al-kaffi wa-al-khamsati aṣābiʿa fa-inna tafsīrahu taʿāla baʿda khamsati ayyāmin
sentences.l: And she said: O son of my uncle, as for her signing with the palm and the five fingers, its interpretation is: Come after five days.
sentences.i: She said, “Cousin, her sign with her palm and five fingers means, ‘Come back in five days.’
sentences.n: ishāratuhā bi-al-kaffi, “her signing with the palm”: bi-, “with”, of the instrument. al-khamsati aṣābiʿa: the numeral in its -a form, which Classical Arabic uses with masculine nouns, here goes with aṣābiʿ, which is usually feminine; that, and the article on the numeral, are both spoken usage. tafsīrahu, “its meaning”: the pronoun is masculine although ishāra, “sign”, is feminine, as if “that sign” were meant.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا إِشَارَتُهَا بِالْمِرْآةِ وَإِدْلَاءِ الْمِنْدِيلِ الْأَحْمَرِ وَرَفْعِهِ وَإِبْرَازِ رَأْسِهَا مِنَ الطَّاقَةِ فَإِنَّ تَفْسِيرَهُ اقْعُدْ عَلَى دُكَّانِ الصَّبَّاغِ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَكَ رَسُولِي
sentences.tr: wa-ammā ishāratuhā bi-al-mirʾāti wa-idlāʾi al-mindīli al-aḥmari wa-rafʿihi wa-ibrāzi raʾsihā mina al-ṭāqati fa-inna tafsīrahu uqʿud ʿalā dukkāni al-ṣabbāghi ḥattā yaʾtiyaka rasūlī
sentences.l: And as for her signing with the mirror, and the letting-down of the red kerchief and its raising, and the putting-forth of her head from the window, its interpretation is: Sit at the shop of the dyer until my messenger comes to you.
sentences.i: And her sign with the mirror, the letting down and drawing up of the red kerchief, and her putting her head out of the window, means, ‘Sit at the dyer's shop until my messenger comes to you.’”
sentences.n: dukkān is the shop front with its bench, where a man may sit; ʿalā, “on”, because one sits on its platform. bi-al-mirʾāti: bi-, “with”, as before.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ كَلَامَهَا اشْتَعَلَتِ النَّارُ فِي قَلْبِي وَقُلْتُ بِاللَّهِ يَابِنْتَ عَمِّي إِنَّكِ تَصْدُقِينَنِي فِي هَذَا التَّفْسِيرِ لِأَنِّي رَأَيْتُ فِى الزُّقَاقِ صَبَّاغًا يَهُودِيًّا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu kalāmahā ishtaʿalati al-nāru fī qalbī wa-qultu bi-allāhi yā-binta ʿammī innaki taṣduqīnanī fī hādhā al-tafsīri li-annī raʾaytu fī al-zuqāqi ṣabbāghan yahūdiyyan
sentences.l: So when I heard her speech, the fire blazed in my heart, and I said: By God, O daughter of my uncle, you are truthful to me in this interpretation, because I saw in the lane a Jewish dyer.
sentences.i: When I heard what she said, the fire blazed up in my heart, and I said, “By God, cousin, you have read it truly, for I did see a Jewish dyer in that lane.”
sentences.n: bi-allāhi, “by God”: bi- of the oath. ṣadaqa, “to speak truly”, takes the person told as a direct object: taṣduqīnanī, “you tell me the truth”. li-annī, “because I”: li-, “for, because”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَيْتُ فَقَالَتِ ابْنَةُ عَمِّي قَوِّ عَزْمَكَ وَثَبِّتْ قَلْبَكَ فَإِنَّ غَيْرَكَ يَشْتَغِلُ بِالْعِشْقِ مُدَّةَ سِنِينَ وَيَتَجَلَّدُ عَلَى حَرِّ الْغَرَامِ وَأَنْتَ لَكَ جُمْعَةٌ فَكَيْفَ يَحْصُلُ لَكَ هَذَا الْجَزَعُ
sentences.tr: thumma bakaytu fa-qālati ibnatu ʿammī qawwi ʿazmaka wa-thabbit qalbaka fa-inna ghayraka yashtaghilu bi-al-ʿishqi muddata sinīna wa-yatajalladu ʿalā ḥarri al-gharāmi wa-anta laka jumʿatun fa-kayfa yaḥṣulu laka hādhā al-jazaʿu
sentences.l: Then I wept, and the daughter of my uncle said: Strengthen your resolve and make-firm your heart, for other-than-you is occupied with love a space of years and bears-up against the heat of passion, and you — you have a week; so how does this despair come to you?
sentences.i: Then I wept, and my cousin said, “Be strong and steady your heart. Others are taken up with love for years on end and bear the heat of passion bravely, and you have been at it a week: how can you have fallen into such despair?”
sentences.n: yashtaghilu bi-al-ʿishqi, “is occupied with love”: ishtaghala takes bi-, “with”, for what one is busy with. jumʿa, the day of Friday prayer, is in spoken Arabic also “a week”, from one Friday to the next; anta laka jumʿatun, “you, you have a week”, is spoken word order. The print writes qawwi and thabbit with their shaddas.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَتْ تُسَلِّينِي بِالْكَلَامِ وَأَتَتْ لِي بِالطَّعَامِ فَأَخَذْتُ لُقْمَةً وَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ آكُلَهَا فَمَا قَدَرْتُ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhat tusallīnī bi-al-kalāmi wa-atat lī bi-al-ṭaʿāmi fa-akhadhtu luqmatan wa-aradtu an ākulahā fa-mā qadartu
sentences.l: Then she began consoling me with talk, and brought me the food; and I took a morsel and wanted to eat it, and could not.
sentences.i: Then she set about comforting me with words, and brought me food; I took a mouthful and tried to eat it, but could not.
sentences.n: akhadhat tusallīnī, “she began consoling me”: akhadha with a following verb means “to begin”. atat lī bi-al-ṭaʿāmi: atā bi-, “to bring”; the verb chooses the bi-.

sentences.t: فَامْتَنَعْتُ مِنَ الشَّرَابِ وَالطَّعَامِ وَهَجَرْتُ لَذِيذَ الْمَنَامِ وَاصْفَرَّ لَوْنِي وَتَغَيَّرَتْ مَحَاسِنِي لِأَنِّي مَا عَشِقْتُ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ وَلَا ذُقْتُ حَرَارَةَ الْعِشْقِ إِلَّا فِي هَذِهِ الْمَرَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-imtanaʿtu mina al-sharābi wa-al-ṭaʿāmi wa-hajartu ladhīdha al-manāmi wa-iṣfarra lawnī wa-taghayyarat maḥāsinī li-annī mā ʿashiqtu qabla dhālika wa-lā dhuqtu ḥarārata al-ʿishqi illā fī hādhihi al-marrati
sentences.l: And I refrained from drink and food, and forsook the sweet of sleep, and my colour yellowed and my beauties changed, because I had not loved before that, nor tasted the heat of love except in this time.
sentences.i: I gave up drink and food and forsook sweet sleep; my colour turned sallow and my good looks faded, for I had never been in love before, nor tasted the heat of passion until now.
sentences.n: al-ṭaʿām … al-manām, “food … sleep”: the narrative falls into rhyme. maḥāsin, “beauties, good features”, is the plural used for a person's looks.

sentences.t: فَضَعُفْتُ وَضَعُفَتْ بِنْتُ عَمِّي مِنْ أَجْلِي
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaʿuftu wa-ḍaʿufat bintu ʿammī min ajlī
sentences.l: So I weakened, and the daughter of my uncle weakened for my sake.
sentences.i: I grew weak, and my cousin grew weak on my account.
sentences.n: The print marks the endings of the two verbs, ḍaʿuftu, “I weakened”, and ḍaʿufat, “she weakened”, so that the same letters are not misread.

sentences.t: وَصَارَتْ تَذْكُرُ لِي أَحْوَالَ الْعُشَّاقِ وَالْمُحِبِّينَ عَلَى سَبِيلِ التَّسَلِّي فِي كُلِّ لَيْلَةٍ إِلَى أَنْ أَنَامَ وَكُنْتُ أَسْتَيْقِظُ فَأَجِدُهَا سَهْرَانَةً مِنْ أَجْلِي وَدَمْعُهَا يَجْرِي عَلَى خَدِّهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārat tadhkuru lī aḥwāla al-ʿushshāqi wa-al-muḥibbīna ʿalā sabīli al-tasallī fī kulli laylatin ilā an anāma wa-kuntu astayqiẓu fa-ajiduhā sahrānatan min ajlī wa-damʿuhā yajrī ʿalā khaddihā
sentences.l: And she took to recounting to me the states of the lovers and the loving, by way of consolation, every night until I slept; and I would wake and find her sleepless for my sake, and her tears running on her cheek.
sentences.i: Every night she would tell me stories of lovers and their fortunes, to comfort me, until I fell asleep; and when I woke I would find her lying awake for my sake, the tears running down her cheek.
sentences.n: ṣārat tadhkuru, “she took to telling”: ṣāra with a following verb means “to begin, to come to do (habitually)”. sahrānatan, “wakeful”, is a spoken feminine of sahrān; Classical would use sahrā.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَزَلْ كَذَلِكَ إِلَى أَنْ مَضَتِ الْخَمْسَةُ أَيَّامٍ فَقَامَتِ ابْنَةُ عَمِّي وَسَخَّنَتْ لِي مَاءً وَحَمَّتْنِي بِهِ وَأَلْبَسَتْنِي ثِيَابِي وَقَالَتْ لِي تَوَجَّهْ إِلَيْهَا قَضَي اللَّهُ حَاجَتَكَ وَبَلَّغَكَ مَقْصُودَكَ مِنْ مَحْبُوبَتِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam azal ka-dhālika ilā an maḍati al-khamsatu ayyāmin fa-qāmati ibnatu ʿammī wa-sakhkhanat lī māʾan wa-ḥammatnī bihi wa-albasatnī thiyābī wa-qālat lī tawajjah ilayhā qaḍā allāhu ḥājataka wa-ballaghaka maqṣūdaka min maḥbūbatika
sentences.l: And I did not cease thus until the five days had passed; then the daughter of my uncle rose and heated water for me and bathed me with it and clothed me in my clothes, and said to me: Go to her; may God fulfil your need and bring you to your aim from your beloved.
sentences.i: So I went on until the five days had passed. Then my cousin got up, heated water and bathed me in it, dressed me in my clothes, and said, “Go to her, and may God grant your wish and bring you what you long for from your beloved.”
sentences.n: ka-dhālika, “thus”: ka-, “like”. al-khamsatu ayyāmin, “the five days”: the article on the numeral, as before. ḥammatnī, “she bathed me”, is a contracted spoken form of ḥammamatnī; bihi: bi-, “with”, of what she used. qaḍā allāhu ḥājataka, “may God fulfil your need”: a past verb used as a wish; the print spells qaḍā with a dotted yā.

sentences.t: فَمَضَيْتُ وَلَمْ أَزَلْ مَاشِيًا إِلَى أَنْ أَتَيْتُ إِلَى رَأْسِ الزُّقَاقِ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ فِي يَوْمِ السَّبْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-maḍaytu wa-lam azal māshiyan ilā an ataytu ilā raʾsi al-zuqāqi wa-kāna dhālika fī yawmi al-sabti
sentences.l: So I went, and did not cease walking until I came to the head of the lane; and that was on the day of the Sabbath.
sentences.i: Off I went, and walked until I reached the top of the lane. That was on a Saturday.
sentences.n: yawm al-sabt is Saturday, the Sabbath, the day on which the Jewish dyer's shop would be shut. ilā an ataytu: after ilā an the past tense is used for what did happen; in Classical usage the subjunctive is more usual.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ دُكَّانَ الصَّبَّاغِ مَقْفُولَةً فَجَلَسْتُ عَلَيْهَا حَتَّى أَذَّنَ الْعَصْرُ وَاصْفَرَّتِ الشَّمْسُ وَأَذَّنَ الْمَغْرِبُ وَدَخَلَ اللَّيْلُ وَأَنَا لَا أَدْرِي لَهَا أَثَرًا وَلَا أَسْمَعُ حِسًّا وَلَا خَبَرًا
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu dukkāna al-ṣabbāghi maqfūlatan fa-jalastu ʿalayhā ḥattā adhdhana al-ʿaṣru wa-iṣfarrati al-shamsu wa-adhdhana al-maghribu wa-dakhala al-laylu wa-anā lā adrī lahā atharan wa-lā asmaʿu ḥissan wa-lā khabaran
sentences.l: And I saw the shop of the dyer locked; so I sat on it until the afternoon called-to-prayer, and the sun yellowed, and the sunset called-to-prayer, and the night came-in, and I not knowing a trace of her, nor hearing a sound nor a news.
sentences.i: I found the dyer's shop locked, and sat on its bench until the call to the afternoon prayer, until the sun turned yellow and the sunset prayer was called and night came on, and still I saw no trace of her and heard no sound and no word.
sentences.n: maqfūlatan, “locked”: the participle is feminine, treating dukkān, “shop”, as feminine, as the spoken language often does; ʿalayhā, “on it”, follows suit. adhdhana al-ʿaṣru, “the afternoon called”, is short for “the call to the afternoon prayer was made”. lahā, “of her”: li- here marks whose trace.

sentences.t: فَخَشِيتُ عَلَى نَفْسِي وَأَنَا جَالِسٌ وَحْدِي فَقُمْتُ وَتَمَشَّيْتُ وَأَنَا كَالسَّكْرَانِ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلْتُ الْبَيْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-khashītu ʿalā nafsī wa-anā jālisun waḥdī fa-qumtu wa-tamashshaytu wa-anā ka-al-sakrāni ilā an dakhaltu al-bayta
sentences.l: And I feared for myself, I sitting alone; so I rose and walked, I like the drunken (man), until I entered the house.
sentences.i: Sitting there alone, I grew afraid for myself; so I got up and walked home like a drunken man, until I came into the house.
sentences.n: khashītu ʿalā nafsī, “I feared for myself”: khashiya ʿalā, “to fear for”. ka-al-sakrāni: ka-, “like”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلْتُ رَأَيْتُ ابْنَةَ عَمِّى عَزِيزَةَ قَائِمَةً وَإِحْدَى يَدَيْهَا قَابِضَةٌ عَلَى وَتَدٍ مَدْقُوقٍ فِى الْحَائِطِ وَيَدُهَا الْأُخْرَى عَلَى صَدْرِهَا وَهِيَ تُصَعِّدُ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَتُنْشِدُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhaltu raʾaytu ibnata ʿammī ʿazīzata qāʾimatan wa-iḥdā yadayhā qābiḍatun ʿalā watadin madqūqin fī al-ḥāʾiṭi wa-yaduhā al-ukhrā ʿalā ṣadrihā wa-hiya tuṣaʿʿidu al-zafarāti wa-tunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And when I entered I saw the daughter of my uncle, ʿAzīza, standing, and one of her two hands gripping a peg driven in the wall, and her other hand on her breast, and she sending-up sighs and reciting these verses:
sentences.i: When I came in, I saw my cousin ʿAzīza standing with one hand gripping a peg driven into the wall and the other on her breast, heaving deep sighs and reciting these verses:
sentences.n: qābiḍatun ʿalā, “gripping”: qabaḍa ʿalā, “to take hold of”. tuṣaʿʿidu al-zafarāti, “she sends up sighs”: a sigh is imagined as rising from the chest. A peg appears again in a moment, at the edge of the īwān; the text does not say whether it is this one.

sentences.t:
وَمَا وَجْدُ اَعْرَابِيَّةٍ بَانَ اَهْلُهَا * فَحَنَّتْ اِلَى بَانِ الْحِجَازِ وَرَنْدِهِ
اِذَا اٰنَسَتْ رَكْبًا تَكَفَّلَ شَوْقُهَا * بِنَارِ قِرَاهُ وَالدُّمُوعِ بِوِرْدِهِ
بِاَعْظَمَ مِنْ وَجْدِىْ بِحِبِّي وَاِنَّمَا * يَرَى اَنَّنِي اَذْنَبْتُ ذَنْبًا بِوُدِّهِ
sentences.tr:
wa-mā wajdu aʿrābiyyatin bāna ahluhā * fa-ḥannat ilā bāni al-ḥijāzi wa-randihi
idhā ānasat rakban takaffala shawquhā * bi-nāri qirāhu wa-al-dumūʿi bi-wirdihi
bi-aʿẓama min wajdī bi-ḥibbī wa-innamā * yarā annanī adhnabtu dhanban bi-wuddihi
sentences.l:
And the longing of a desert-woman whose people have gone-away, so that she yearns for the ben-trees of the Ḥijāz and its rand —
When she glimpses a riding-party, her longing takes-charge of the fire of its guest-meal, and the tears (take charge) of its watering —
is not greater than my longing for my beloved; yet he sees that I sinned a sin by loving him.
sentences.i:
The longing of a Bedouin girl whose people have gone, who pines for the ben-trees of the Ḥijāz and its sweet rand,
who, when she sees riders far off, lets her longing light the fire to feed them and her tears supply them water —
is no greater than my longing for my love; and yet he thinks that loving him has been my sin.
sentences.n: The three lines are one sentence: wa-mā wajdu …, “the longing of … is not”, waits for its predicate until bi-aʿẓama, “greater”, in the last line, where bi- is the bi- that follows a negative mā and adds only emphasis. The bān (ben-tree, moringa) and the rand (a fragrant desert shrub, sometimes said to be the bay) are the classic plants of the Arabian homeland in love poetry. qirā is the meal given to a guest; wird, the watering-place or the water drawn. The girl alone in the desert sees travellers and, in her longing for her people, her own fire and tears provide their welcome. bi-nāri … bi-wirdihi: bi- after takaffala, “to take charge of, undertake”. bi-ḥibbī, “for my beloved”: bi- after wajd, “longing for”. bi-wuddihi, “by loving him”: bi- of the cause.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا الْتَفَتَتْ إِلَيَّ فَرَأَتْنِى فَمَسَحَتْ دُمُوعَهَا وَدُمُوعِي بِكُمِّهَا وَتَبَسَّمَتْ فِي وَجْهِي وَقَالَتْ لِي يَا بْنَ عَمِّى هَنَّاكَ اللَّهُ بِمَا أَعْطَاكَ فَلِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ لَمْ تَبِتِ اللَّيْلَةَ عِنْدَ مَحْبُوبَتِكَ وَلَمْ تَقْضِ مِنْهَا أَرَبَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā iltafatat ilayya fa-raʾatnī fa-masaḥat dumūʿahā wa-dumūʿī bi-kummihā wa-tabassamat fī wajhī wa-qālat lī yā-bna ʿammī hannāka allāhu bi-mā aʿṭāka fa-li-ayyi shayʾin lam tabiti al-laylata ʿinda maḥbūbatika wa-lam taqḍi minhā arabaka
sentences.l: So when she had finished her verse she turned to me and saw me, and wiped her tears and my tears with her sleeve, and smiled in my face, and said to me: O son of my uncle, may God make-wholesome for you what He gave you! So for what thing did you not pass the night with your beloved, and not fulfil from her your desire?
sentences.i: When she had finished her poem she turned and saw me; she wiped her tears and mine with her sleeve, smiled at me and said, “Cousin, may God bless you in what He has given you! Why did you not spend the night with your beloved and have your desire of her?”
sentences.n: hannāka allāhu, “may God make it wholesome for you”, is the spoken form of hannaʾaka, with the hamza dropped; the print marks its shadda. bi-mā aʿṭāka: bi-, “in, with”, of what is blessed. fa-li-ayyi shayʾin, “for what thing, why”: li-, “for”, of the reason. qaḍā arabahu, “he fulfilled his need”, is plain about the desire meant.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ كَلَامَهَا رَفَصْتُهَا بِرِجْلِي فِي صَدْرِهَا فَانْقَلَبَتْ عَلَى الْإِيوَانِ فَجَاءَتْ جَبْهَتُهَا عَلَى طَرَفِ الْإِيوَانِ وَكَانَ هُنَاكَ وَتَدٌ فَجَاءَ فِي جَبْهَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu kalāmahā rafaṣtuhā bi-rijlī fī ṣadrihā fa-inqalabat ʿalā al-īwāni fa-jāʾat jabhatuhā ʿalā ṭarafi al-īwāni wa-kāna hunāka watadun fa-jāʾa fī jabhatihā
sentences.l: So when I heard her speech, I kicked her with my foot in her breast, and she toppled onto the dais, and her forehead came upon the edge of the dais; and there was a peg there, and it came into her forehead.
sentences.i: When I heard what she said, I kicked her in the chest, and she fell back onto the raised floor; her forehead struck its edge, where there was a peg, and the peg went into her forehead.
sentences.n: rafaṣa, “to kick”, is a spoken form of rafasa. bi-rijlī: bi-, “with”, of the instrument. The īwān is the raised part of a room, a dais or alcove floor; jāʾat … ʿalā and jāʾa fī, literally “came upon” and “came into”, are the spoken way of saying “struck” and “went into”.

sentences.t: فَتَأَمَّلْتُهَا فَرَأَيْتُ جَبِينَهَا قَدِ انْفَتَحَ سَالَ دَمُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-taʾammaltuhā fa-raʾaytu jabīnahā qadi infataḥa sāla damuhā
sentences.l: And I looked-closely at her, and saw her brow had split open, her blood flowed.
sentences.i: I looked at her closely, and saw that her brow had split open and her blood was flowing.
sentences.n: sāla damuhā, “her blood flowed”, follows with no “and”: the print may have dropped a و, or the clause may simply follow on, as speech allows. It is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
